SOME APPLICATIONS OF
TRIGONOMETRY 9

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 9.1 Heights and Distances

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous chapter, you have studied about trigonometric ratios. In this chapter,
you will be studying about some ways in which trigonometry is used in the life around
you.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider Fig. 8.1 of previous chapter, which is redrawn below in Fig. 9.1.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this figure, the line AC drawn from the eye of the student to the top of the
minar is called the \textit{line of sight}. The student is looking at the top of the minar. The
angle BAC, so formed by the line of sight with the horizontal, is called the \textit{angle of}
\textit{elevation} of the top of the minar from the eye of the student.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, the **line of sight** is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point
in the object viewed by the observer. The **angle of elevation** of the point viewed is

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the point being viewed is
above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise our head to look at the object
(see Fig. 9.2).

**Object**

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.2

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, consider the situation given in Fig. 8.2. The girl sitting on the balcony is
looking down at a flower pot placed on a stair of the temple. In this case, the line of
sight is below the horizontal level. The angle so formed by the line of sight with the
horizontal is called the angle of depression.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, the **angle of depression** of a point on the object being viewed is the angle
formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the point is below the horizontal
level, i.e., the case when we lower our head to look at the point being viewed
(see Fig. 9.3).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, you may identify the lines of sight, and the angles so formed in Fig. 8.3.
Are they angles of elevation or angles of depression?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us refer to Fig. 9.1 again. If you want to find the height CD of the minar
without actually measuring it, what information do you need? You would need to know
the following:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (i) the distance DE at which the student is standing from the foot of the minar

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(ii) the angle of elevation, $\angle$ BAC, of the top of the minar
(iii) the height AE of the student.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Assuming that the above three conditions are known, how can we determine the
height of the minar?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In the figure, CD = CB + BD. Here, BD = AE, which is the height of the student.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To find BC, we will use trigonometric ratios of $\angle$ BAC or $\angle$ A.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In $\Delta$ ABC, the side BC is the opposite side in relation to the known $\angle$ A. Now,
which of the trigonometric ratios can we use? Which one of them has the two values
that we have and the one we need to determine? Our search narrows down to using
either $\tan A$ or $\cot A$, as these ratios involve AB and BC.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB}$ or $\cot A = \frac{AB}{BC}$, which on solving would give us BC.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: By adding AE to BC, you will get the height of the minar.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now let us explain the process, we have just discussed, by solving some problems.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Example 1 :** A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground,
which is 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the
tower is found to be $60^{\circ}$. Find the height of the tower.

**Solution :** First let us draw a simple diagram to
represent the problem (see Fig. 9.4). Here AB
represents the tower, CB is the distance of the point
from the tower and $\angle ACB$ is the angle of elevation.
We need to determine the height of the tower, i.e.,
AB. Also, ACB is a triangle, right-angled at B.

To solve the problem, we choose the trigonometric
ratio $\tan 60^{\circ}$ (or $\cot 60^{\circ}$), as the ratio involves AB
and BC.

Now, $\tan 60^{\circ} = \frac{AB}{BC}$

i.e., $\sqrt{3} = \frac{AB}{15}$

i.e., $AB = 15\sqrt{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, the height of the tower is $15\sqrt{3}$ m.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : An electrician has to repair an
electric fault on a pole of height 5 m. She needs
to reach a point 1.3m below the top of the pole
to undertake the repair work (see Fig. 9.5). What
should be the length of the ladder that she should
use which, when inclined at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to
the horizontal, would enable her to reach the
required position? Also, how far from the foot
of the pole should she place the foot of the
ladder? (You may take $\sqrt{3} = 1.73$)

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.5

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : In Fig. 9.5, the electrician is required to
reach the point B on the pole AD.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\text{BD} = \text{AD} - \text{AB} = (5 - 1.3)\text{m} = 3.7 \text{ m.}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, BC represents the ladder. We need to find
its length, i.e., the hypotenuse of the right triangle BDC.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, can you think which trigonometric ratio should we consider?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: It should be $\sin 60^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\frac{\mathrm{BD}}{\mathrm{BC}} = \sin 60^{\circ}$ or $\frac{3.7}{\mathrm{BC}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\text{BC} = \frac{3.7 \times 2}{\sqrt{3}} = 4.28 \text{ m (approx.)}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: i.e., the length of the ladder should be 4.28 m.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $\frac{\text{DC}}{\text{BD}} = \cot 60^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $DC = \frac{3.7}{\sqrt{3}} = 2.14 \text{ m (approx.)}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, she should place the foot of the ladder at a distance of $2.14 \text{ m}$ from
the pole.

blocks.text: SOME APPLICATIONS OF TRIGONOMETRY

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 : An observer 1.5 m tall is 28.5 m away
from a chimney. The angle of elevation of the top
of the chimney from her eyes is $45^\circ$. What is the
height of the chimney?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Here, AB is the chimney, CD the
observer and $\angle$ ADE the angle of elevation (see
Fig. 9.6). In this case, ADE is a triangle, right-angled
at E and we are required to find the height of the
chimney.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.6

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We have $AB = AE + BE = AE + 1.5$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $DE = CB = 28.5 \text{ m}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To determine AE, we choose a trigonometric ratio, which involves both AE and
DE. Let us choose the tangent of the angle of elevation.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $\tan 45^{\circ} = \frac{AE}{DE}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AE = 28.5$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So the height of the chimney (AB) = (28.5 + 1.5) m = 30 m.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : From a point P on the ground the angle of elevation of the top of a 10 m
tall building is $30^{\circ}$. A flag is hoisted at the top of the building and the angle of elevation
of the top of the flagstaff from P is $45^{\circ}$. Find the length of the flagstaff and the
distance of the building from the point P. (You may take $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : In Fig. 9.7, AB denotes the height of the building, BD the flagstaff and P
the given point. Note that there are two right triangles PAB and PAD. We are required
to find the length of the flagstaff, i.e., DB and the distance of the building from the
point P, i.e., PA.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since, we know the height of the building AB, we
will first consider the right $\Delta$ PAB.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We have $\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{AB}{AP}$

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.7

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{10}{AP}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AP = 10\sqrt{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: i.e., the distance of the building from P is $10\sqrt{3}$ m = 17.32 m.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Next, let us suppose $\text{DB} = x \text{ m}$. Then $\text{AD} = (10 + x) \text{ m}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, in right $\Delta$ PAD, $\tan 45^{\circ} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AP}} = \frac{10 + x}{10\sqrt{3}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $1 = \frac{10 + x}{10\sqrt{3}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $x = 10 \left(\sqrt{3} - 1\right) = 7.32$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the length of the flagstaff is $7.32$ m.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:

Example 6 : The angles of depression of the top and the bottom of an 8 m tall building
from the top of a multi-storeyed building are $30^{\circ}$
and $45^{\circ}$, respectively. Find the height of the multi-
storeyed building and the distance between the
two buildings.

Solution : In Fig. 9.9, PC denotes the multi-
storeyed building and AB denotes the 8 m tall
building. We are interested to determine the height
of the multi-storeyed building, i.e., PC and the
distance between the two buildings, i.e., AC.
Look at the figure carefully. Observe that PB is
a transversal to the parallel lines PQ and BD.
Therefore, $\angle QPB$ and $\angle PBD$ are alternate
angles, and so are equal.
So $\angle PBD = 30^{\circ}$. Similarly, $\angle PAC = 45^{\circ}$.
In right $\Delta PBD$, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\frac{\mathrm{PD}}{\mathrm{BD}} = \tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \quad \text{or} \quad \mathrm{BD} = \mathrm{PD} \sqrt{3}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In right $\Delta$ PAC, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\frac{\mathrm{PC}}{\mathrm{AC}} = \tan 45^{\circ} = 1$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e.,                                     $PC = AC$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, $\text{PC} = \text{PD} + \text{DC}$, therefore, $\text{PD} + \text{DC} = \text{AC}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Since, $\mathrm{AC} = \mathrm{BD}$ and $\mathrm{DC} = \mathrm{AB} = 8 \mathrm{~m}$, we get $\mathrm{PD} + 8 = \mathrm{BD} = \mathrm{PD}\sqrt{3}$ (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: This gives $\quad \text{PD} = \frac{8}{\sqrt{3} - 1} = \frac{8(\sqrt{3} + 1)}{(\sqrt{3} + 1)(\sqrt{3} - 1)} = 4(\sqrt{3} + 1) \text{ m.}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the height of the multi-storeyed building is $\{4(\sqrt{3} + 1) + 8\}m = 4(3 + \sqrt{3})m$

and the distance between the two buildings is also $4(3 + \sqrt{3})m$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: and the distance between the two buildings is also $4(3 + \sqrt{3})\mathrm{m}$.

blocks.text: EXERCISE 9.1

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. A circus artist is climbing a 20 m long rope, which is
tightly stretched and tied from the top of a vertical
pole to the ground. Find the height of the pole, if
the angle made by the rope with the ground level is
$30^{\circ}$ (see Fig. 9.11).

2. A tree breaks due to storm and the broken part
bends so that the top of the tree touches the ground
making an angle $30^{\circ}$ with it. The distance between
the foot of the tree to the point where the top
touches the ground is 8 m. Find the height of
the tree.

3. A contractor plans to install two slides for the children to play in a park. For the children
below the age of 5 years, she prefers to have a slide whose top is at a height of 1.5 m, and
is inclined at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ to the ground, whereas for elder children, she wants to have
a steep slide at a height of 3m, and inclined at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to the ground. What
should be the length of the slide in each case?

4. The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point on the ground, which is 30 m
away from the foot of the tower, is $30^{\circ}$. Find the height of the tower.

5. A kite is flying at a height of 60 m above the ground. The string attached to the kite is
temporarily tied to a point on the ground. The inclination of the string with the ground
is $60^{\circ}$. Find the length of the string, assuming that there is no slack in the string.

6. A 1.5 m tall boy is standing at some distance from a 30 m tall building. The angle of
elevation from his eyes to the top of the building increases from $30^{\circ}$ to $60^{\circ}$ as he walks
towards the building. Find the distance he walked towards the building.

7. From a point on the ground, the angles of elevation of the bottom and the top of a
transmission tower fixed at the top of a 20 m high building are $45^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$ respectively.
Find the height of the tower.

blocks.label: Question

**8.** A statue, 1.6 m tall, stands on the top of a pedestal. From a point on the ground, the
angle of elevation of the top of the statue is $60^{\circ}$ and from the same point the angle of
elevation of the top of the pedestal is $45^{\circ}$. Find the height of the pedestal.

angle of elevation of the top of the tower from the foot of the building is $60^{\circ}$. If the tower
is 50 m high, find the height of the building.

which is 80 m wide. From a point between them on the road, the angles of elevation of
the top of the poles are $60^{\circ}$ and $30^{\circ}$, respectively. Find the height of the poles and the
distances of the point from the poles.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 9.2 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
**1. (i) The line of sight** is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the
object viewed by the observer.

(ii) The **angle of elevation** of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight
with the horizontal when it is above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise
our head to look at the object.

(iii) The **angle of depression** of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight
with the horizontal when it is below the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we lower
our head to look at the object.

**2. The height or length of an object or the distance between two distant objects can be**
determined with the help of trigonometric ratios.
